```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r libs}
library(topolow)
library(ggplot2)

output_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "h3n2_bootstrap")
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## What this does

The usual topolow workflow fits parameters once and builds one map. Both steps
then depend on the particular panel of sera that happened to be in the assay.

This script does both steps over **random subsets of the sera, keeping every
virus**:

1. parameter optimization draws a fresh subset of sera for each evaluation
   (`opt_subsample_sera`), and
2. the map is built many times on serum subsets, and the estimated distances are
   averaged cell by cell, with a standard deviation and a replicate count
   (`bootstrap_embedding()`).

**Why only the sera are drawn.** One can object that a scheme which never drops
a virus says nothing about how much the viruses influence one another's
positions. But no pair of viruses is ever measured against each other: the
assay titrates viruses against sera, so the virus-virus block of the matrix is
empty, and every virus-virus relation in the map is reconstructed through the
sera that both viruses were titrated against. Their influence on each other
travels through the references, so varying which references are present varies
the whole set of measurements through which one virus can constrain another.
Resampling both sides would be the more complete design, and this one does
leave out the variability contributed by the choice of virus panel; in
practice, varying the subset of references while preserving all the viruses
covers the majority of the uncertainty in positions that the choice of sample
induces.

Drawing is **without replacement**. Resampling sera *with* replacement would put
two identical rows in the submatrix, which the force model reads as a pair of
points with a measured dissimilarity of zero, and would inflate the degree of
every virus titrated against that serum. The scheme implemented here is
*m*-out-of-*n* subsampling, equivalently a delete-*d* jackknife.

## 1. Data

```{r data}
data(h3n2_data, package = "topolow")

processed <- process_antigenic_data(
  data        = h3n2_data,
  antigen_col = "virusStrain",
  serum_col   = "serumStrain",
  value_col   = "titer",
  is_similarity = TRUE,
  metadata_cols = c("cluster", "color", "virusYear", "serumYear")
)
dist_mat <- processed$matrix

# The steps below split the points themselves, on the "V/" and "S/" prefixes
# that process_antigenic_data() writes; this call only reports that split.
groups <- identify_antigens_sera(dist_mat)
c(points = nrow(dist_mat),
  antigens = length(groups$antigens),
  sera = length(groups$sera))
```

The matrix is 285 x 285 over 216 viruses and 69 sera, and it is of **character**
mode because thresholded titres are carried as strings such as `"<10"`.

A note on cost: keeping all 216 viruses and dropping 20% of 69 sera removes only
14 of 285 points, so serum subsampling buys very little speed here. What it
removes is about a fifth of the *measurements*, and what it changes is which
serum panel the parameters are fitted to. The speed argument for `opt_subsample`
does not transfer; the robustness argument does.

## 2. Parameter optimization over serum subsets

This stage is the expensive one: every likelihood evaluation runs `folds`
embeddings. Run it once and keep the result.

```{r optimisation, eval=FALSE}
param_ranges <- list(
  N_min = 2, N_max = 10,
  k0_min = 1, k0_max = 20,
  cooling_rate_min = 1e-4, cooling_rate_max = 0.05,
  c_repulsion_min = 1e-4, c_repulsion_max = 0.02
)

scenario_name <- "h3n2_sera_bootstrap"

initial <- initial_parameter_optimization(
  dissimilarity_matrix = dist_mat,
  mapping_max_iter = 500,
  relative_epsilon = 1e-4,
  convergence_counter = 2,
  scenario_name = scenario_name,
  N_min = param_ranges$N_min, N_max = param_ranges$N_max,
  k0_min = param_ranges$k0_min, k0_max = param_ranges$k0_max,
  c_repulsion_min = param_ranges$c_repulsion_min,
  c_repulsion_max = param_ranges$c_repulsion_max,
  cooling_rate_min = param_ranges$cooling_rate_min,
  cooling_rate_max = param_ranges$cooling_rate_max,
  num_samples = 50,
  folds = 20,
  opt_subsample_sera = 0.8,   # every virus kept, 80% of sera drawn
  write_files = TRUE,
  output_dir = output_dir,
  verbose = TRUE
)

samples_file <- file.path(output_dir, "model_parameters",
                          paste0(scenario_name, "_model_parameters.csv"))

run_adaptive_sampling(
  initial_samples_file = samples_file,
  scenario_name = scenario_name,
  dissimilarity_matrix = dist_mat,
  num_samples = 150,
  mapping_max_iter = 500,
  relative_epsilon = 1e-4,
  folds = 20,
  opt_subsample_sera = 0.8,
  output_dir = output_dir,
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

Each evaluation now sees a different serum panel of the same size, so the
likelihoods stay comparable while the chosen parameters stop depending on any
one serum.

### Picking the optimum

```{r pick, eval=FALSE}
samples <- read.csv(samples_file)
samples <- samples[is.finite(samples$NLL) & is.finite(samples$Holdout_MAE), ]
samples <- as.data.frame(lapply(samples, clean_data, k = 3))
samples <- na.omit(samples)

best <- samples[which.min(samples$Holdout_MAE), ]
optimal_params <- list(
  N            = round(exp(as.numeric(best$log_N))),
  k0           = exp(as.numeric(best$log_k0)),
  cooling_rate = exp(as.numeric(best$log_cooling_rate)),
  c_repulsion  = exp(as.numeric(best$log_c_repulsion))
)
print(optimal_params)

# The subset size is a fixed count, recorded with every evaluation. Read it
# back so the bootstrap in section 3 draws subsets of exactly the same size.
n_sera_used <- unique(na.omit(samples$opt_n_sera))
stopifnot(length(n_sera_used) == 1)
n_sera_used

# Convergence of the search itself
plot_mcmc_diagnostics(chain_files = samples_file, mutual_size = 500,
                      save_plot = FALSE)
```

## 3. The bootstrapped map

The parameters below are the ones already fitted for this dataset in
`inst/examples/parameter-fitting-h3n2.Rmd`. Replace them with the output of
section 2 when you have run it.

```{r params}
optimal_params <- list(
  N            = 5,
  k0           = 6.862815,
  cooling_rate = 0.02549249,
  c_repulsion  = 0.01039692
)

# Section 2 would give this as n_sera_used. 0.8 x 69 sera = 55.
n_sera_used <- 55
```

```{r bootstrap}
set.seed(2026)

boot <- bootstrap_embedding(
  dissimilarity_matrix = dist_mat,
  ndim         = optimal_params$N,
  k0           = optimal_params$k0,
  cooling_rate = optimal_params$cooling_rate,
  c_repulsion  = optimal_params$c_repulsion,
  mapping_max_iter = 1000,
  relative_epsilon = 1e-6,
  n_replicates = 500,
  n_sera       = n_sera_used,   # the same fixed count the search used
  random_seed  = 2026,
  verbose      = TRUE
)

# Every replicate drew the same number of points
table(boot$replicates$n_points)

summary(boot)
```

### The three matrices

`est_distances` is the deliverable: the full virus-and-serum distance matrix,
each cell averaged over the replicates in which both of its endpoints were
present.

```{r matrices}
boot$est_distances[1:5, 1:5]   # mean
boot$sd_distances[1:5, 1:5]    # standard deviation
boot$n_obs[1:5, 1:5]           # replicates behind each cell
```

Coverage differs by block, so summarise the blocks separately rather than
putting them on one scale: virus-virus cells appear in every replicate,
virus-serum cells in about `frac_sera` of them, and serum-serum cells in about
`frac_sera^2`. A useful rule is `n_replicates >= 30 / frac_sera^2`.

```{r write, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(boot$est_distances, file.path(output_dir, "h3n2_mean_distances.csv"))
write.csv(boot$sd_distances,  file.path(output_dir, "h3n2_sd_distances.csv"))
write.csv(boot$n_obs,         file.path(output_dir, "h3n2_counts.csv"))
```

### Did dropping sera distort the geometry?

Dropping sera removes springs while leaving the virus-virus repulsion count
unchanged, so the configuration can expand slightly. The calibration table
regresses the bootstrap means on a single full-data embedding, per block. A
`slope0` near 1 means the two agree.

```{r calibration}
boot$calibration
```

## 4. Drawing the uncertainty

Uncertainty regions cannot come from `sd_distances`. A distance matrix is
invariant to rotation, so it carries no directional information and could only
give a circle. `bootstrap_embedding()` therefore also keeps each replicate's
coordinates, rigidly aligned to the full-data map, and those give properly
elongated regions.

```{r coords}
coords <- data.frame(boot$positions)
names(coords) <- paste0("V", seq_len(ncol(boot$positions)))
coords$name      <- rownames(boot$positions)
coords$antigen   <- startsWith(coords$name, "V/")
coords$antiserum <- startsWith(coords$name, "S/")
coords$year      <- as.numeric(sub(".*/([0-9]{4}).*", "\\1", coords$name))

# Cluster metadata travels with h3n2_data
meta <- unique(h3n2_data[, c("virusStrain", "cluster", "color")])
meta$name <- paste0("V/", meta$virusStrain)
coords <- merge(coords, meta[, c("name", "cluster", "color")],
                by = "name", all.x = TRUE)
coords$cluster[is.na(coords$cluster)] <- "serum"
coords$cluster <- factor(coords$cluster)
```

```{r plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Regions are drawn for the antigens only by default: a region on all 285
# points at once buries the map. Pass uncertainty_points = "all" to see them.
p_time <- plot_temporal_mapping(
  coords, ndim = optimal_params$N,
  uncertainty = boot,
  uncertainty_conf_level = 0.68,
  uncertainty_points = "antigens"
)
p_time

p_clust <- plot_cluster_mapping(
  coords, ndim = optimal_params$N,
  uncertainty = boot,
  uncertainty_conf_level = 0.68,
  uncertainty_points = "antigens"
)
p_clust
```

`bootstrap_blobs()` returns the same polygons as a data frame if you would
rather draw them yourself, and offers a kernel-density contour in place of the
default covariance ellipse:

```{r blobs}
blobs <- bootstrap_blobs(boot, conf_level = 0.68, method = "ellipse")
head(blobs)
```

## 5. What the standard deviations do and do not mean

**They mix two sources.** One is the serum-panel variability we are after. The
other is topolow's own run-to-run variability: the C++ backend reshuffles its
sweep order using a generator independent of R's RNG, so repeated runs on an
identical matrix do not give identical coordinates. On this dataset the second
component is not negligible. Measure it directly by rerunning with every serum
kept, which leaves only the optimizer randomness:

```{r nullarm, eval=FALSE}
null_arm <- bootstrap_embedding(
  dissimilarity_matrix = dist_mat,
  ndim = optimal_params$N, k0 = optimal_params$k0,
  cooling_rate = optimal_params$cooling_rate,
  c_repulsion = optimal_params$c_repulsion,
  mapping_max_iter = 1000, relative_epsilon = 1e-6,
  n_replicates = 100, frac_sera = 1, random_seed = 7
)

ut <- upper.tri(boot$sd_distances)
data.frame(
  source = c("serum subsampling + optimizer", "optimizer only"),
  median_sd = c(median(boot$sd_distances[ut], na.rm = TRUE),
                median(null_arm$sd_distances[ut], na.rm = TRUE))
)
```

**They are the spread at the subsample size**, not the sampling standard
deviation of the full-data estimate. For that reading, multiply by the
finite-population factor, which the object reports but never applies:

```{r jackknife}
boot$settings$jackknife_factor   # sqrt(f / (1 - f)); exactly 1 at frac_sera = 0.5
```

**They cover one source of uncertainty only.** The virus panel is held fixed in
every replicate, and measurement error in the titres themselves is not
represented at all. Sera are also treated as exchangeable; if they cluster by
eliciting strain, pass a hand-built `sample_pool` to draw whole groups instead.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
unlink(output_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```
